title: Saw “Gerry” (2002, Gus Van Sant) today. Can’t stop thinking about it.

commenti.body:
I really liked that movie. It made me laugh and get giddy—someone *made* this? So great, how did this even get made?

It's one of those intentional slow burn movies. Sort of like early Jim Jarmusch, but just in that slow, spare pacing and nothing else. 

It's not really about the plot, it's sort of loose and left out there as raw material for each individual viewer to make something with. I wouldn't go to deep into other people's "something" though.

I was on spring break in Paris when it came out, me and my friends didn't know anything about it but we felt like going to a movie some random night and walked into this one. It was such a fun experience because we were the only ones laughing at all the weird ticcy language, "shirt basket?" etc. But also the movie just floored me, haunting beautiful, textured, it's been a long time since I've seen it so it's hard to say much more about it, gotta see it again soon now, thank you
Dirt mattress.
Gus Van Sant is heavily influenced by Bela Tarr especially in this film. If you're interested in slow cinema and haven't seen Bela Tarr's films I'd recommend Werckmeister Harmonies!

Gus van Sant’s  other films he made at this time also were exercises in pace and time. 

I always thought there was an absurdity about these experiences (specifically the tenants of the theatre of the absurd: Time passing, waiting for an inevitable death or god, silence, repetition, irrational speech.) 

Slow cinema is so engaging. I too get lost in the experience and find my own sense of time passing is warped. His film Last Days is another patient treatment of life and death. If you are entranced by Gerry I read that it was a homage to Satantango, a 7 hour film that is both amazing beautiful and filled with existential dread.

As others have already gestured at, van Sant made other, similar films around the same time, what he called his "death trilogy": this, then Elephant (about a Columbine-style school shooting), and finally Last Days (about the last days and suicide of a barely at all veiled Kurt Cobain type character). They're all terrific, and I especially like Elephant, which is a quietly devastating exercise in restrained naturalism; Last Days is funny to watch if you're in the right mood. The trilogy overall is the highlight of van Sant's career, and all of them with cinematography by the late, great Harris Savides

Others have mentioned "slow cinema" but Gerry belongs to an even more specific sub-genre: "slow walking cinema", slow movies with a lot of loooooooong silent takes of people walking. See also not just Satantango, but also Meek's Cutoff and Loneliest Planet (both great films, too!)

*Gerry* was one of those I-have-the-t.v.-late-at-night-because-everyone-else-is-asleep-which-is-cool-but-I-can't-turn-the-volume-up-or-it'll-wake-people-up-and-that's-cool-so-I-have-to-put-the-subtitles-on.

Luckily... you don't really need subtitles for *Gerry.*  I was able to watch it and fully get it.  And honestly, for those that would struggle to watch it because it's "boring," I get it.  But somehow Damon and Affleck can hold my attention for 90-110 minutes just walking.  I'm not saying it's "entertaining" but it catches my attention so it's "something." 

Somehow *that* was more watchable than *Last Days.*

I don't have some great in-depth analysis.  (I never do for this sub anyway because... I don't know.  I'm not smart enough, honestly.)  For me >!the whole film was a lead up to Affleck's death and Damon's choice to participate in it and his ensuing rescue and his reaction in the end.!<  That's it.  That's the film.  The whole film is built up until the last like 5 minutes.  And it makes the film.

And there's something about the shot Van Sant likes where figures are walking in a aimlessly in a wide space.  Same goes for the dudes playing that video game in *Elephant.*  I like those shots too.  I don't question why he held on it for like 5 min.
The new “experimental” horror film “In a Violent Nature” also features a lot of Bela Tarr-esque walking through nature. And bursts of violence.

I saw an interview where Van Sant commented that he'd gotten into video games before he made Gerry and he was into the idea that in video games you don't see as many cuts. He talked about how if you want to travel in a video game, you experience the whole trip. 

That made me think about Gerry in a different way...

Right?

I didn’t even look at the year of production when I came across this on Prime today. Just read “lost” and “death valley” and hoped it wasn’t one I’d seen before. Getting lost or stuck is my favorite movie niche.
I’ll check them out! Thank you.

Wow. I’ll check out your recommendation 

It’s amazing how intentional certain creative decisions are when you look back, right? Viewing this was a disorienting experience. Then I realized, practically speaking, how long would that desert experience have taken in real life? I don’t think they could go more than two days without water, especially in those temps. But the cinematography made time transcend for me.
I saw that “Ina a Violent Nature” came up a few times when reading about “Gerry.” I need to check it out.

I loved it. It has the basic plot, dialogue, and acting of a bad Friday the 13th pic from the 80s but it’s shot in the style of an art-house film and follows the killer instead of the victims. Perfect for weirdos like me who loves art-house AND grind-house films!

I loved Gerry. Just the dudes walking side by side was so weirdly hypnotic as it seemed so natural with their little noises and look arounds. Just some lovely moments of pure cinema - nothing really happening just enjoying the frame before you. You start to feel the dread building as they get more lost and the relaxed walk becomes out of their control. I thought the ending was ridiculous though - killed a bit of "fascination with nothingness' going on with its melodramatic, unrealistic ending.

Wow - makes sense now:

In Gus Van Sant's *Elephant*, one of the characters plays the Gerry video game:

https://youtu.be/JRbrfG-cP3M?si=1UJvxj5pwJLezSnm
103 minutes actually

When my wife and I (who are generally Gus Van Sant fans) saw it in the theater it was prefaced by our local film geeks talking about Sant’s admiration for Bela Tarr, who was just getting international exposure at the time (late 90s/early aughts). That of course led me to Bela Tarr, who I now love. I think that helped adjust our expectations a bit. The whole thing being framed as Sant and his famous actor buddies making an opaque artsy movie in the desert that was inspired by an almost-impenetrable type of filmmaker (at least to Hollywood-bred audiences) like Tarr put it all into perspective. Did we like it? Our gut reaction was it felt like something better suited to the MoMa. But it definitely became a running gag for us: anytime either of us makes an egregious mistake we say we totally gerried that thing. Ultimately the humor…very dry humor…saves it. I love that they made it, then Sant went on to hone his Tarr-esque schtick for Elephant and Paranoid Park and Last Days.

Not sure if the version you watched lets you know in the credits the different locations this was filmed in. Apparently shot in at least three or four deserts across the globe, which helps lend it that anywhere/everywhere lost quality. Dang I want to rewatch it now!
That is super interesting!!

You are most welcome! As others have said there is a plethora of “slow cinema” to sink into. 

(I personally love Lav Diaz - however his movies are rooted in the Phillipines and their political situation. It’s harrowing storytelling - much more dialogue - but when it transcends space and time, characters are meandering through empty streets with no real purpose. He defiantly uses pace and time to make you feel what it is like to live under those political
conditions.) 

I totally agree it’s disorienting - My understanding of those choices I think are made to make the audience feel time passing the way the characters do, and in turn communicates how our relationship to time informs our psychology and inner world. 

Putting those characters in a literal desert is also an another way to remove time - when they walk through that space there are no landmarks; sand is always shifting and footsteps can disappear. It’s like the perfect location to loose yourself in but also evokes the notion of seeking or looking for something. 

Viewing Gerry, I remember I was super into Gus Vant sant and you’ve made me want to revisit the film.
I love this. Thank you for sharing how you interpret this art!

Yes. Such beautiful imagery. And excellent observations about cinematography decisions. As to your last sentence, I get where you’re coming from. I encourage you to search for an alternate explanation for that ending! I’m not big on alternative theories. But once I read it, it was a major “ah! Of course that’s a possibility!”
